extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democratic institutions, political associations, and comparative government
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of Tocqueville's evaluative principles about democratic institutions (associations, suffrage, elections, public officers) as presented in Democracy in America. Focuses on norms, causes, examples, and dangers Tocqueville identifies for healthy democratic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of political association as a necessary check
rubrics_metrics.description: The right of association is 'a necessary guarantee against the tyranny of the majority' and is almost as inalienable as personal liberty; no legislator can attack it without impairing society's foundations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Associations serve as an artificial substitute for missing aristocratic bodies and are essential in democracies to oppose the physical power of a preponderant party with moral authority. Example: conventions (e.g., Convention of 1831) may be necessary but are serious occurrences. Warning: legislators should not suppress the right of association; it prevents conspiracies where associations are free.

rubrics_metrics.name: Associations should be peaceable, legal, and deliberative (not militarized)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the United States political associations 'are peaceable in their intentions, and strictly legal in the means which they employ'; they aim to persuade rather than to fight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American associations primarily 'show their numerical strength', 'stimulate competition', and 'discover those arguments which are most fitted to act upon the majority.' Anti-patterns (European model): associations formed as armies, centralizing power, using watchwords, enforcing passive obedience, abjuring personal judgment — these lead to tyrannical internal control and loss of moral force. Positive model: associations borrow civil administrative forms, recognize individual independence, and exert reason and will for common ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of association reduces secret societies and conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Where associations are free, secret societies are unknown: 'In America there are numerous factions, but no conspiracies.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing open, lawful association channels diffuses clandestine plotting. Suppressing lawful association tends to drive political activity underground and toward conspiratorial forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal suffrage does not guarantee wise choice of leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Universal suffrage 'is by no means a guarantee of the wisdom of the popular choice' — the most able men are rarely placed at the head of affairs under broad democracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reasons: the mass lacks time and means for deep inquiry; democratic institutions foster envy and a passion for equality that undermines respect for legitimate superiority; education, manners, and social stability affect electoral judgment (contrast New England vs new South-west). Exception: in periods of grave danger the people often select extraordinary leaders. Overall implication: universal suffrage can yield competent choices under certain conditions (education, crisis), but is not intrinsically sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect election/election by an elected body refines selection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate (elected by elected bodies) contains a higher proportion of celebrated men than the House (directly elected by the populace); 'this transmission of the popular authority through an assembly of chosen men operates an important change' by refining discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism: having an intermediate elected body moderate popular impulses and select representatives who 'represent the elevated thoughts' of the community. Tocqueville recommends introducing election by an elected body more frequently to mitigate democratic weaknesses and raise the level of governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of elections: trade-off between revolution and mutability
rubrics_metrics.description: When elections are rare the State risks violent crises; when frequent they produce 'feverish excitement' and legislative mutability. Americans have preferred frequent elections and accept instability rather than revolutionary danger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy trade-off: rare elections -> high-stakes, violent struggle when they occur; frequent elections -> continual instability and changing laws/policy. Cited authorities: Hamilton (fear of 'facility and excess of law-making' and mutability) and Jefferson (proposal to require a year between introduction and final passage of bills to reduce instability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public officers should be simple, accessible, and remunerated
rubrics_metrics.description: American public officers display a simple exterior (no official costume), are accessible, civil, remunerated, and integrated with citizens; 'All public officers are remunerated' in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: remuneration enables broad participation and prevents public charges being limited to the wealthy (which would create an aristocracy). A shift from unpaid to paid offices (or vice versa) signals significant constitutional change: unpaid offices becoming paid indicates movement toward more democratic or despotic forms, while making previously paid offices gratuitous indicates drift toward monarchical/aristocratic institutions. Also, the absence of pomp does not undermine respect for office when the officeholder's merit suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: No permanent public career where election extends to every office
rubrics_metrics.description: In democracies where election extends to every place, 'no political career can, properly speaking, be said to exist'; men are promoted as if by chance and may not retain rank, so public functions offer few lures to ambition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: many ordinary men occupy public stations; the pursuit of wealth diverts talented individuals from public life; talented men often do not come forward, reducing the pool of high-caliber officeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitrary power of magistrates is pronounced in democracies
rubrics_metrics.description: Magistrates exercise considerable arbitrary power both in absolute monarchies and in democratic republics; under a democracy the arbitrary power of the magistrate 'must be still greater' than in despotic States because the majority grants latitude of action and expects adaptability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: In democracies the people, able to remove officers at will, prefers leaving them latitude rather than imposing invariable rules; this fosters broader discretionary authority for magistrates. Implication: democratic systems need safeguards against excessive arbitrariness even while allowing administrative flexibility.
